previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a long history of mast cell activation syndrome was admitted for a typical flare characterized by chest pain, wheezing, dyspnea, and diffuse discomfort. She presented to the emergency department after symptoms became intolerable, with no identifiable trigger. Initial evaluation, including chest X-ray and EKG, showed no acute cardiopulmonary issues, and labs were within normal limits. She was treated with her established IV regimen of Benadryl, Dilaudid, and Ativan every four hours, with gradual improvement in symptoms. An ipratropium inhaler was added to manage wheezing, as she preferred to avoid albuterol due to anxiety. Her other conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, orthostatic hypotension, and mood disorders, remained stable, with home medications continued. She expressed emotional distress about the chronic nature of her illness and was encouraged to follow up with her primary doctor, rheumatologist, and a psychiatrist. By discharge, she was ambulatory, breathing comfortably, and able to manage symptoms on oral medications.

Brief Hospital Course:
 Mrs ___ is a ___ y/o female with Mast-Cell Degranulation 
Syndrome who was admitted with a flare of her usual symptoms 
attributed to this condition which include SOB, wheezing, 
pruritus, chest pain, headache and epigastric pain. She has had 
numerous prior admissions with the same symptoms most recently 
in ___.  She was treated with IV Dilaudid + Ativan + 
Diphenhydramine which is the usual combination of medication she 
receives on her admissions as well as albuterol nebs and 
Fioricet.
While her symptoms on her current admission were consistent with 
a flare of Mast Cell Deg Syn, upon observation, there was also 
an impression of a possible psychological element to her 
complaints: behaviors such as deep breathing, psychomotor 
agitation and arm scratching were often noted while the patient 
was being examined but not when one watched the patient 
unobserved. This may be related to narcotic dependence and/or 
secondary gain. This may also explain her response to Dilaudid 
and Ativan which  would probably not otherwise be particularly 
beneficial for Mast Cell Degranulation Syndrome per se. Mrs. 
___ was treated as above with gradual resolution of her 
complaints. She was discharged without change to her chronic 
medication regimen and will continue follow-up with her PCP.
